_note: General contract-review guidance written for LeaseLens. These entries are NOT laws, regulations or legal citations. Rules differ between countries, states and cities, so every entry is general guidance only.

entries.title: Automatic renewal and cancellation windows
entries.summary: Some agreements renew for a new term unless you cancel within a set window before the end date. Missing the window can lock you in for another full term.
warning_signs: same terms for a further period
entries.example_clause: This agreement shall automatically renew for successive twelve month terms unless either party gives ninety days written notice before expiry.
questions: What is the exact last date I can cancel to avoid renewal?
Can renewal be changed to opt-in instead of automatic?
Will the price change when the agreement renews?

entries.title: Price changes at renewal
entries.summary: A renewal clause may allow new prices or terms to start with the new term. Check how much notice you get about changes before the renewal deadline passes.
warning_signs: renewal at the then current rate
entries.example_clause: Upon renewal the rent shall be adjusted to the landlord's then current market rate.
questions: How will the renewal price be set?
Will I be told about new terms before my cancellation deadline?

entries.title: Deposit deductions should be specific
entries.summary: Clear deposit clauses say which costs can be deducted, how damage is documented, and when the remainder is returned. Vague wording gives the other side wide room to keep money.
entries.example_clause: The landlord may retain all or part of the deposit for any reason at its sole discretion.
questions: Which specific costs can be deducted from the deposit?
Will we do a move-in and move-out inspection together with photos?
How many days after move-out will the deposit be returned?

entries.title: Non-refundable payments
entries.summary: A payment labelled non-refundable will usually not come back, even if you leave early or the deal falls through. Make sure you understand what it pays for.
entries.example_clause: A non-refundable cleaning deposit of 500 will be charged at signing.
questions: What exactly does this non-refundable payment cover?
Is it refundable if the agreement does not start?

entries.title: Extra fees on top of the main price
entries.summary: Administrative, processing, service or amenity fees can noticeably raise the real cost. A fair contract lists each fee with an amount or a clear formula.
entries.example_clause: Tenant shall pay a monthly amenity fee and any additional charges as determined by management.
questions: Can you list every fee with its amount?
Can any fee increase during the agreement?
What is the total monthly cost including all fees?

entries.title: Open-ended cost sharing
entries.summary: Clauses that pass on utilities, maintenance or other costs without a cap or a method of calculation make your total cost hard to predict.
entries.example_clause: Tenant shall reimburse landlord for a proportionate share of all building operating costs.
questions: How is my share calculated?
Is there a cap on these costs?
Can I see past bills?

entries.title: Balanced termination rights
entries.summary: Check whether both sides can end the agreement on similar terms. One-sided rights, very short notice for the other side, or long notice for you are worth discussing.
entries.example_clause: The company may terminate this agreement at any time without notice, while the employee must give three months notice.
questions: Can both of us end the agreement with the same notice period?
What reasons allow termination without notice?

entries.title: Cost of leaving early
entries.summary: Early termination may require paying the remaining rent or balance, or a fixed fee. Understand the maximum you could owe if your plans change.
entries.example_clause: If tenant terminates early, tenant shall pay all remaining rent for the full term.
questions: What is the most I would owe if I need to leave early?
Is the amount reduced if a replacement tenant is found?
Can a fixed early-exit fee replace the remaining-rent requirement?

entries.title: Late charges should be predictable
entries.summary: A late charge is common, but daily percentages, compounding charges or very short grace periods can grow quickly. Look for a grace period and a maximum.
entries.example_clause: A late charge of 5% per day shall apply to any unpaid amount.
questions: Is there a grace period before late charges start?
Is there a maximum late charge?
How is the late charge calculated?

entries.title: Fixed penalties and forfeitures
entries.summary: Fixed penalty amounts or forfeiture of money already paid should be proportionate to the actual harm. Large fixed amounts deserve a closer look.
entries.example_clause: Breach of any term shall result in forfeiture of all amounts paid and a penalty equal to two months salary.
questions: What situations trigger this penalty?
Can the penalty be reduced or capped?

entries.title: Indemnity and hold-harmless clauses
entries.summary: An indemnity can make you pay the other side's losses, claims or legal fees, sometimes even when you were not at fault. Check the scope and whether it is mutual.
entries.example_clause: Tenant shall indemnify and hold harmless the landlord from all claims, losses and legal fees arising from the premises.
questions: Is the indemnity limited to losses I actually cause?
Is the indemnity mutual?
Is there a cap on the amount?

entries.title: Broad exclusions of the other side's responsibility
entries.summary: Clauses saying the other side is not responsible for any damage or loss can shift all risk to you. Consider whether insurance or exceptions for negligence are needed.
warning_signs: shall not be liable for any
entries.example_clause: The landlord shall not be liable for any damage to tenant's property for any reason.
questions: Are you responsible if damage is caused by your negligence or a building defect?
Which repairs am I responsible for, exactly?
Do I need my own insurance?

entries.title: One side can change the terms
entries.summary: If one side can change prices, rules or terms without your consent, the agreement you sign may not be the agreement you end up with. Ask for notice and a right to exit.
entries.example_clause: The company reserves the right to modify these terms at any time at its sole discretion.
questions: Will I get written notice before any change?
Can I end the agreement without penalty if I do not accept a change?
Which terms can never change during the agreement?

entries.title: Price increases during the term
entries.summary: Clauses allowing rent, fees, interest or pay to be adjusted should explain how often, by how much, and with what notice.
entries.example_clause: Rent may be increased by the landlord during the lease term.
questions: How often and by how much can the amount change?
How much notice will I receive before an increase?

entries.title: Waiving rights
entries.summary: Some contracts ask you to give up rights or claims. Depending on where you live, some waivers may not be allowed, but you should not rely on that without advice.
entries.example_clause: Tenant waives all rights to withhold rent for any reason.
questions: Which rights am I giving up, exactly?
Can this waiver be removed or narrowed?

entries.title: Access and use restrictions
entries.summary: Entry without notice, bans on guests, or limits on subletting affect daily life. Check that access rules give reasonable notice except in emergencies.
entries.example_clause: The landlord may enter the premises at any time without notice.
questions: How much notice will you give before entering, except in emergencies?
Are short visits from guests allowed?

entries.title: Vague or open-ended wording
entries.summary: Phrases like 'including but not limited to', 'reasonable costs' or 'as deemed necessary' can be read broadly. Ask for concrete examples, amounts or limits.
entries.example_clause: Tenant shall pay reasonable costs as deemed necessary by the landlord from time to time.
questions: Can you give specific examples or a maximum amount?
Who decides what is reasonable?

entries.title: Conflicting clauses
entries.summary: Words like 'notwithstanding anything else' can override other promises in the same document. Check which clause wins if two clauses disagree.
entries.example_clause: Notwithstanding anything in this agreement, the employer may withhold any payment.
questions: Which clauses does this override?
Can the overriding wording be removed or limited?

entries.title: Non-compete scope
entries.summary: A non-compete limits future work. Check the duration, geography and type of work it covers. Enforceability varies widely between places.
entries.example_clause: For two years after leaving, the employee shall not work for any competitor anywhere in the world.
questions: How long does the restriction last and where does it apply?
Which companies or roles are covered?
Is there any payment during the restricted period?

entries.title: Non-solicitation
entries.summary: Non-solicitation clauses limit contacting clients or colleagues. Check whether they cover people you knew before joining.
entries.example_clause: The employee shall not solicit any client of the company for three years.
questions: Does this cover clients I worked with before joining?
How long does it last?

entries.title: Variable interest and compounding
entries.summary: Variable rates and frequent compounding change your total cost. Ask for the total amount payable and an example with a rate increase.
entries.example_clause: Interest shall be charged at a variable rate compounded monthly.
questions: What is the total amount I will pay over the full term?
How high can the rate go?
How often is interest compounded?

entries.title: Early repayment and acceleration
entries.summary: Prepayment charges make it costly to pay early, and acceleration clauses can make the whole balance due after one missed payment. Check the triggers.
entries.example_clause: Upon any default, the entire outstanding balance shall become immediately due and payable.
questions: What counts as a default?
Is there a cure period before the full balance becomes due?
What does early repayment cost?

entries.title: Arbitration and dispute forums
entries.summary: Arbitration clauses send disputes to a private process instead of court. Check who pays the costs, where it happens, and whether small claims court is still allowed.
entries.example_clause: All disputes shall be resolved by binding arbitration and the parties waive any right to a jury trial.
questions: Who pays for arbitration?
Can small disputes still go to a local court?

entries.title: Governing law and location
entries.summary: A clause choosing another region's law or courts can make disputes expensive to pursue. Check whether it matches where you live or work.
entries.example_clause: This agreement is governed by the laws of a different state and disputes must be heard only in its courts.
questions: Why is this location chosen?
Can disputes be heard where I live?
